description_en: A cello concerto in a single movement, unusual in that its three sections are played without a break. It shows off both the cello's virtuosity and its lyricism.
By far the most famous of all Bruch's works. One of the great masterpieces of the Romantic violin concerto, it is ranked alongside the concertos of Mendelssohn and Brahms.
A four-movement fantasy for violin and orchestra built on Scottish folk melodies. It is loved no less than Bruch's violin concerto.
A meditative short piece for cello and orchestra, composed on the melody of the chant 'Kol Nidrei', which is sung on the Jewish Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur).
An intermezzo from Act 2 of the opera Thaïs. This devout, beautiful violin solo portrays the meditation of the dancer Thaïs, who has been converted by the monk Athanaël.
A French lyric opera based on Goethe's The Sorrows of Young Werther. It portrays the tragic love of its title character with great delicacy.

Sarasate's signature work. It is built from a melancholy melody of Hungarian Gypsy (Roma) music (lassan) and a dance that grows ever more fiery (friska), and is the ultimate showpiece of violin virtuosity.
A fantasy built on famous melodies from Bizet's opera Carmen (the Habanera, the Seguidilla and others), with brilliant violin virtuosity added.
A brilliant short piece that shows off fast violin technique: a slow introduction is followed by the tarantella, a fiery Italian dance.
No. 1 of Elgar's five Pomp and Circumstance Marches. The majestic melody of the middle section (Land of Hope and Glory) is so famous that it is called Britain's 'second national anthem'.

Elgar's last major work. An introspective, mournful piece that carries the sense of loss and grief after the First World War. It was rediscovered in the 20th century through the playing of cellist Jacqueline du Pré.
A unique work in which each of the 14 variations portrays a friend or acquaintance in Elgar's circle. The theme of the 'enigma' has still not been solved. Variation 9, 'Nimrod', is especially famous.
A sweet short piece for violin (or cello) that Elgar composed to mark his engagement to Caroline Alice Roberts. It is very popular with the general public.
Leoncavallo's only success and a leading work of 'verismo' (realist) opera. Its shocking story: a clown who learns of his wife's infidelity kills her on the theatre stage.
The aria that closes Act 1 of Pagliacci, sung in anguish by the clown Canio, who must go on stage even though he knows his wife has betrayed him. One of the most famous tenor arias.
An Italian song (canzone) by Leoncavallo. Its bright, brilliant melody sings of the splendour of the morning, and tenors love to perform it.
Originally a piano piece, it evokes the flamenco technique of the Spanish guitar so perfectly that it is now better known as a guitar solo.
Albéniz's masterpiece and one of the most difficult works in the history of piano music. Twelve pieces capture the impressions and moods of the various regions of Spain.
The second of the six pieces in the suite España. Its exotic, enchanting melody has led to arrangements for many instruments, and it is a much-loved short piece.
Winner of a one-act opera competition, it opened the era of 'verismo' (realist) opera. Set in Sicily, it tells a story of passion and revenge among ordinary people.
The tragic and beautiful intermezzo played in the middle of the opera. It became more famous than the opera itself and has been used in countless media, including the film The Godfather Part III.
A symphonic poem that stirred the patriotism of the Finnish people resisting Russian oppression. The solemn, beautiful hymn in the middle section is called Finland's de facto national anthem.
One of the greatest violin concertos composed in the 20th century. It combines the cold, majestic nature of northern Europe with the extreme technical demands of the violin.
One of the pieces of incidental music for the play Kuolema. An eerie yet beautiful waltz depicting the vision of a dying mother dancing with ghosts.
The most popular and most Romantic of Sibelius's symphonies. It opens with melodies that seem to depict the nature of northern Europe and ends with a majestic, heroic finale.
A masterpiece based on a hymn melody by the 16th-century composer Thomas Tallis, in which two string orchestras and a string quartet create a mysterious sound.
An orchestral fantasy based on the famous English folk song 'Greensleeves'. It is marked by a lyrical, pastoral mood.
A romance for solo violin and orchestra, inspired by a poem by George Meredith. It portrays a lark soaring into the sky in lyrical fashion.
A seven-movement orchestral suite depicting the astrological character of seven planets (Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune). 'Mars' and 'Jupiter' are especially famous.
A string ensemble piece that Holst wrote for the student orchestra of St Paul's Girls' School, where he taught. The English folk song 'Greensleeves' appears in the fourth movement.
An essential collection of etudes for beginning pianists. Titles with a Romantic sensibility, such as 'Arabesque', 'Pastorale' and 'Ballade', make it very popular.
A step up from Op. 100, this collection of etudes, with titles such as 'Pearls' and 'Storm', demands more brilliant technique and greater expressiveness.
The only piece by Rubinstein still known today, a short piano work. Its sweet melody made it hugely popular as 19th-century salon music.
In its day it was counted as the leading Russian piano concerto before Rachmaninoff, but it is almost never played now, an ill-fated masterpiece.
Wieniawski's signature work. Brilliant violin virtuosity is balanced with Polish-flavoured Romantic melodies reminiscent of Chopin (the Romance, second movement).
A work that expresses the Polish dance, the polonaise, through brilliant violin virtuosity. It is often played as an encore to show off a violinist's skill.
A short piece for violin and orchestra with a striking mysterious, wistful melody. It represents Wieniawski's lyricism.
A work that shows the essence of the guitar's tremolo technique (rapid repeated plucking of a single string). It is dreamlike, as if depicting the sound of the fountains of the Alhambra palace.
Composed by Tárrega after he travelled in Andalusia in southern Spain (a region influenced by Arab culture). Its exotic, plaintive melody is characteristic.
Wolf's first major song collection, setting 53 poems by the poet Eduard Mörike. 'Im Frühling' and 'Der Verborgene' are among the famous songs.
A collection of 46 songs based on Paul Heyse's volume of translated Italian folk poetry. Within a short, compressed form it holds wit and depth, and it is a masterpiece of Wolf's later years.

The most famous of Nielsen's symphonies. Composed amid the turmoil of the First World War, it expresses the 'unquenchable will to live'. The passage in which two timpani seem to fight a fierce battle is striking.
One of the great clarinet concertos of the 20th century. It explores the clarinet's technique and expressiveness to the limit and is marked by a sharp confrontation with the snare drum.

Glazunov's most famous work. It follows the tradition of the Romantic concerto but is distinguished by its single-movement design, played without a break. It is loved for its lyrical, brilliant melodies.
A ballet in three acts set in the age of the medieval Crusades. Full of brilliant, exotic melodies, including Hungarian-style dances, it is an important part of the classical ballet repertoire.
Reger's best-known orchestral work. Based on the theme of the first movement of Mozart's Piano Sonata No. 11 (K. 331), it varies the theme with the rich harmony and counterpoint of late Romanticism.
A grand and complex organ work built on the 'B-A-C-H' motif (B♭-A-C-B♮). It concentrates Reger's reverence for Bach and his contrapuntal skill.
A ballet based on a legend of the Andalusian Gypsies of Spain. The 'Ritual Fire Dance' (Danza ritual del fuego) is very famous for its fiery rhythm.
Composed for the Ballets Russes, with sets and costumes by Picasso. A masterpiece that makes modern use of Spanish folk dances (jota, fandango and others).
'Symphonic impressions' for piano and orchestra, depicting the night scenery and impressions of the gardens of Spain (Andalusia). Debussy's Impressionist influence is strongly evident.

A revolutionary work that announced the beginning of 20th-century music. It depicts a primitive pagan Russian ritual, and its radical dissonances and primitive, explosive rhythms caused a scandal at the Paris premiere in 1913.

Stravinsky's first success with the Ballets Russes. It is marked by brilliant, exotic orchestration that shows the influence of his teacher Rimsky-Korsakov. The 'Dance of the Firebird' and 'Infernal Dance' are famous.
A ballet telling the tragic love story of three puppets (Petrushka, the Ballerina and the Moor). Its 'polytonality' technique, in which different keys sound at the same time, was innovative.
A sacred choral work representing Stravinsky's 'neoclassical' period. Set to the Latin text of the Psalms, it combines medieval grandeur with a modern rhythmic feel.

Schoenberg's early masterpiece in the late-Romantic style. A symphonic poem for string sextet (later arranged for string orchestra), it is marked by Wagnerian intense chromaticism and emotional expression.
A work representing Schoenberg's 'atonal' period. It is marked by the distinctive vocal technique called Sprechstimme (speech-like singing) and a grotesque Expressionist atmosphere.
A cantata for narrator, chorus and orchestra based on the testimony of a survivor of the Nazi ghetto. Composed using the twelve-tone technique, it is a shocking and dramatic work.
Works written just before Schoenberg established the twelve-tone technique. In the fifth piece, 'Waltz', the technique is used in part for the first time.

Composed by Shostakovich, who was in danger of being purged after Stalin's regime condemned his opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District, as 'an artist's response to criticism'. On the surface it conforms to the regime, but beneath lies a joy forced by coercion (tragedy).
A symphony composed while Nazi Germany besieged Leningrad. The relentlessly repeated 'invasion theme' of the first movement is famous, and the work became a symbol of the Soviet spirit of resistance.

Shostakovich's most popular melody. Long thought to belong to the lost Jazz Suite No. 2, it is now classified as part of the Suite for Variety Stage Orchestra No. 1. It was used in the film Bungee Jumping of Their Own.
An autobiographical work that takes the composer's initials as its theme: the motif D-S-C-H (D-E♭-C-B). Dedicated to the victims of fascism, it is the most intense and anguished of his chamber works.
A masterpiece of the 20th-century cello concerto, written for Mstislav Rostropovich. It is marked by extreme cello virtuosity, the D-S-C-H motif and fierce rhythms.
The finest ballet music of the 20th century, based on Shakespeare's tragedy. The menacing melody of the 'Dance of the Knights' (Montagues and Capulets) is especially famous.
A leading work of 'neoclassicism', in which Prokofiev reinterpreted Haydn's style in a 20th-century manner. Witty and light, it has a finale (fourth movement) whose sense of speed is the highlight.

A musical fairy tale composed to introduce children to the instruments of the orchestra. Each character is portrayed by a particular instrument: Peter (strings), the bird (flute), the wolf (horn) and so on.
The most brilliant and popular of the 20th-century piano concertos. Sharp rhythms, a percussive piano and lyrical melodies are combined.
One of three 'war sonatas' composed during the Second World War. The mechanical, violent finale (third movement) in 7/8 is overwhelming.
Bartók's greatest masterpiece, composed during his exile in the United States. Every instrument of the orchestra shows off brilliant skill, like the soloist of a concerto.

A masterpiece of 20th-century orchestral music that concentrates Bartók's originality. It is marked by a symmetrical movement structure (the golden section), an unusual instrumentation and folk rhythms. It was used in the film The Shining.
A one-act ballet that caused a scandal at its premiere because of its violent, lurid content. It is marked by primitivist, fierce rhythms.
A collection of 153 piano exercises that Bartók wrote for his son Péter. Beginning with simple pieces, it lets the player learn step by step up to the complex techniques of 20th-century modern music.
Considered the greatest series of string quartets since Beethoven. A monument of 20th-century chamber music, it concentrates Bartók's compositional technique and his research into folk music.
A symbolic work of American music that combines classical music and jazz. It opens with the famous clarinet glissando (sliding note), and the brilliant piano virtuosity stands out.
The first great American opera, set in a poor Black neighbourhood. All of its arias, beginning with 'Summertime', have become jazz and blues standards.
A symphonic poem depicting the impressions Gershwin gathered while travelling in Paris. Jazzy blues melodies and the sound of Parisian car horns (taxi horns) blend delightfully.
A full-scale three-movement concerto written after the success of Rhapsody in Blue. It combines the form of the Romantic concerto with the idiom of jazz.

A musical that transposes Romeo and Juliet to a conflict in modern New York between a Puerto Rican immigrant gang (the Sharks) and a white gang (the Jets). 'Mambo' and 'Tonight' are among the famous numbers.
An arrangement of the musical's main dances as a symphonic suite. Jazz and Latin rhythms and fierce orchestration stand out.
The overture to the operetta based on Voltaire's satirical novel Candide. Witty and brilliant, it is a staple of American orchestras' repertoire.

A symphony in two parts and six movements, inspired by a poem by W. H. Auden. The piano plays a role as important as in a concerto, and the work portrays the loneliness and faith of modern people after the Second World War.
The national anthem of South Korea. Composed around 1935, it was adopted as the official anthem when the South Korean government was established in 1948.
A symphonic poem composed after Ahn Eak-tai studied with Richard Strauss. Built on late-Romantic orchestration, it develops the melody of the 'Aegukga' (national anthem) as its main theme.
Composed in 1920, the first Korean art song (gagok). Its plaintive melody sings of the sorrow of the people under Japanese colonial rule through the image of the balsam flower.
A children's song beloved by the whole nation, beginning with the words 'The home where I used to live...'. Set to a poem by Lee Won-su, it is regarded as the archetype of Korean lyricism.
Composed in 1921, the oldest surviving original Korean work for violin. According to an anecdote, it holds Hong Nan-pa's own tragic love story.
An opera based on the classic Korean novel Simcheongjeon. Premiered as the opening work of the cultural festival of the 1972 Munich Olympics, it brought Isang Yun worldwide fame.

A masterpiece that reveals Isang Yun's deep understanding of the cello. He conceived it while imprisoned after the East Berlin Affair, and the cello's sobbing 'nonghyeon' technique (a Korean way of wavering the pitch) is outstanding.
Based on the idea of 'ye-ak' (ritual and music), a representative orchestral work by Isang Yun that realises the solemn, slow breathing of court music with a Western orchestra.
Piano etudes that create an original sound by combining the twelve-tone technique with the sigimsae (ornamentation) and grace notes of Korean traditional music.
The first of a triptych of staged cantatas, composed on secular poems found in a medieval monastery. Primitive, intense rhythms are its hallmark.
The chorus that opens and closes Carmina Burana. With its majestic, overwhelming melody singing of the whims of the goddess Fortune, it is the most famous piece of 20th-century classical music.

John Cage's most famous and most controversial work. For 4 minutes 33 seconds the performer sits in front of an instrument (usually a piano) and plays nothing. It presents 'sound within silence' (the noise of the audience and so on) as music.
Screws, rubber, bolts and the like are inserted between the strings of the piano to make a 'prepared piano', and the work uses it to pursue percussive, Eastern-sounding timbres.
A grand work in four acts and five hours that opened the era of 'minimalist opera'. An innovative work made up of repeating figures and images, with no plot.
One of the most famous of Philip Glass's piano etudes. It is characterized by an endlessly repeating right-hand arpeggio and shifting left-hand harmonies.
Music composed for the film The Hours. Glass's characteristic repeating piano figures effectively conveyed the film's melancholy, introspective mood.
An educational masterpiece that introduces every instrument of the orchestra (woodwinds, brass, strings and percussion) through variations and a fugue on a theme by Purcell.
The greatest masterpiece of 20th-century English opera. It portrays the tragedy of Peter Grimes, a fisherman isolated from his village. The four 'Sea Interludes' are especially famous.

The finest requiem of the 20th century, composed for the rebuilding of Coventry Cathedral, which was destroyed in the Second World War. It interleaves the text of the traditional Latin Mass with the anti-war poems of the First World War poet Wilfred Owen.
The first of three cello suites composed for the cellist Mstislav Rostropovich, inspired by Bach's unaccompanied cello suites.

A chamber work composed and premiered in a German prisoner-of-war camp during the Second World War. With its unusual instrumentation of violin, cello, clarinet and piano, it depicts the 'end of time' of the Book of Revelation in a mystical way.
A set of twenty piano pieces that view the birth of the infant Jesus through twenty different gazes (the Virgin Mary, angels, stars and so on). It is the essence of Messiaen's piano music.
A huge symphony in ten movements, whose title means 'love, time, life' and the like in Sanskrit. A piano and the 'ondes Martenot' (an early electronic instrument) are used as solo instruments.
Thirteen piano pieces composed on birdsong that Messiaen transcribed throughout France. An original work that reproduces birdsong on the piano.
The greatest masterpiece of 20th-century Expressionist opera. In atonal music it portrays how the poor soldier Wozzeck is gradually driven mad by social oppression, commits murder and is destroyed.
Berg's last work, left behind at his death. Although it uses the twelve-tone technique, it combines a Bach chorale with Romantic lyricism to express deep sorrow and beauty.
A suite in six movements for string quartet. Composed with the twelve-tone technique, it is a passionate, lyrical work that holds Berg's secret declaration of love.

The peak of Webern's twelve-tone technique. Played by only nine instruments, it is marked by extremely restrained 'pointillist' sound and a symmetrical structure. Its running time is about 10 minutes.
An early work from Webern's 'atonal' period. It consists of five extremely short (aphoristic) movements and is a radical short work that destroys traditional harmony and form.
An orchestral work from the atonal period. Each movement is very short, and timbre itself (Klangfarbenmelodie) is treated as an important element of the music.
Ives's most famous and most philosophical work. Over hushed strings (silence), a trumpet poses 'the question of existence', and the woodwinds answer it in confusion (mockery).

Ives's most experimental large-scale work, in which complex rhythms, polytonality and collage techniques are all deployed. It was so complex that it was not given a complete premiere until 1965, fifty years after it was composed.

A piano sonata in four movements portraying the American Transcendentalist thinkers (Emerson, Hawthorne, Alcott and Thoreau). It is filled with extremely difficult, experimental techniques (dissonance, atonality).

An orchestral suite depicting three places in New England in the United States (a Revolutionary War monument, Putnam's Camp and the Housatonic River). Its 'collage' technique, in which several melodies sound at once, is famous.
Piazzolla's signature work, which introduced his 'nuevo tango' to the world. A compound of 'Libertad' (freedom) and 'tango', it announces a new style that breaks away from traditional tango.
A piece loved for having one of the most lyrical and plaintive melodies of all Piazzolla's works. It was used on the soundtrack of the film Enrico IV.
Composed in memory of his father's death, and Piazzolla himself counted it as his 'finest work'. Fierce rhythms and anguished melodies alternate.
A tango-version response to Vivaldi's The Four Seasons. It portrays the four seasons of Buenos Aires in four tango works ('Winter', 'Spring', 'Summer', 'Autumn').

Satie's most famous piano piece. The first of three short pieces written while imagining the festivals of ancient Greece (the gymnopédies). Simple and dreamlike, it is regarded as a forerunner of minimalism.
One of six short piano pieces inspired by the ancient Cretan palace (Knossos). Like the Gymnopédies, it creates a mysterious, exotic atmosphere.
A popular chanson (waltz) that Satie composed for a cabaret singer. It shows Satie's cheerful, sentimental side.
A fierce dance of Armenian warriors from the last act of the ballet Gayane. Along with 'Boléro' and 'O Fortuna', it is one of the greatest hits of 20th-century classical music.
A ballet in three acts about the revolt of the Roman gladiator Spartacus. The 'Adagio of Spartacus and Phrygia' is famous for its sensual, grand melody.
A brilliant violin concerto full of the exotic melodies and rhythms of Armenian folk music. It is one of the major concertos of the 20th-century repertoire.
A suite arranged from the incidental music for Lermontov's play Masquerade. The 'Waltz' movement is especially famous.
Nam June Paik's early avant-garde music. It consists of various written instructions instead of a score, and is made up of actions such as smashing a piano or shouting.
A representative action piece from his Fluxus period. Instead of playing, the performer slowly lifts the violin and smashes it down on a table.
An early piano work composed under the influence of John Cage's 'prepared piano'.
A gagok set to a poem by Lee Eun-sang, and one of the best-loved gagok among Koreans. It portrays longing for his hometown (Masan) in a Romantic, grand melody.
A gagok set to a poem by Jo Yeong-chul. Beginning with the words 'Oh, my beloved magnolia', it is a brilliant, passionate song of the mood of spring and of love.
A gagok set to a poem by Kim Dong-hwan. It opens with the words 'My heart is a lake' and is a lyrical song of love like a calm lake.
Kim Dong-jin's representative orchestral work. Composed in 1968, it combines Korean melodies with Romantic orchestration.
Janáček's most famous orchestral work. It is marked by a brilliant first movement in which nine trumpets sound a fanfare, and it symbolizes the might of the Czech army and the freedom of Brno.
The opera that raised Janáček to the ranks of the world's composers. A masterpiece of 'realist' opera that grafts the 'speech intonation' of the Moravian region onto the melody.
A fairy-tale-like, philosophical opera in which the world of forest animals and the world of humans intersect. It holds Janáček's love of nature and his idea of the cycle of life.
An original setting of the Mass that uses a text in Old Church Slavonic (Glagolitic) instead of the traditional Latin Mass. Janáček's Pan-Slavism and intense expressiveness stand out.
The most famous of the nine Bachianas Brasileiras. With its unusual scoring for an ensemble of eight cellos and a solo soprano, it is famous above all for its first movement, 'Aria (Cantilena)'.
The first of the twelve guitar etudes (W 235). Dedicated to the guitarist Andrés Segovia, it is essential repertoire for guitar majors.
The first of the fourteen Chôros. A solo guitar piece that captures the features of indigenous Brazilian folk music.
The last (fourth) movement of Bachianas Brasileiras No. 2, a suite in four movements for orchestra. It cheerfully depicts the sound of a small country steam locomotive.
A symphony in three movements reworked from the music of Hindemith's opera of the same name, Mathis der Maler. It was inspired by the work of the Renaissance painter Matthias Grünewald.
An orchestral work based on themes from Carl Maria von Weber's forgotten piano duets, brilliantly varied with Hindemith's characteristic neoclassical technique.
The most famous of the three viola sonatas left by Hindemith, who was himself a violist. It is at the core of the 20th-century viola repertoire.
Poulenc's greatest operatic masterpiece. It deals with the true story of the Carmelite nuns who chose martyrdom during the French Revolution. The chorus in the final guillotine scene is shocking.
Sacred music for solo soprano, chorus and orchestra. One of the masterpieces of 20th-century choral music, in which devotion and characteristically French wit coexist.
An early piano piece by Poulenc, influenced by Satie. A charming piece in which simple, witty melodies repeat endlessly (perpetual motion).
The most important and most frequently performed of the 20th-century flute sonatas. The flute's lyricism and Poulenc's characteristic lightness and melancholy are in perfect harmony.

The most important work in the history of electronic music. The first 'spatial music', it combines a boy's altered voice (musique concrète) with pure electronic sounds (synthesizer) through five loudspeakers.
A 'meditation music' for a vocal ensemble of six. The singers sing a low B♭ using overtone technique, creating a mysterious sound.

Act 3 of the opera Wednesday from Light. The four members of a string quartet each play from a separate helicopter in the air, and the sound is transmitted to the ground, making this an avant-garde work.

A representative work of late-20th-century 'postmodernist' music. A symphony in five movements for eight voices and orchestra. In the third movement in particular, a great deal of music (Bach, Beethoven, Debussy and others) and text is layered by collage technique over Mahler's Symphony No. 2.

No. 3 of the fourteen Sequenzas, a series exploring the virtuosity of solo instruments. A performance-art piece that dramatically expresses every sound the female voice can make (laughter, whispers, coughs, screams and others).
Berio's most popular collection: eleven folk songs from around the world, including the United States, Armenia, France and Italy, arranged for mezzo-soprano and chamber ensemble.
Lutosławski's early masterpiece and his best-known work. Like Bartók's work of the same name, it is based on Polish folk songs, and every instrument of the orchestra shows off brilliant technique.
Variations for two pianos on Paganini's Caprice No. 24. Composed to be played in cafés during the Second World War, it is counted a masterpiece of 20th-century arrangement.

A masterpiece that concentrates the composer's late technique of 'limited aleatoricism'. It is marked by passages in which the conductor gives only the broad framework and the players improvise the detailed rhythms.
The main theme of Francis Ford Coppola's Godfather trilogy. Immortal film music that holds both the melancholy of Sicily and the ruthlessness of the Mafia.
The main theme of Franco Zeffirelli's film Romeo and Juliet. Also famous as the song 'A Time for Us', it shows romantic melody at its height.
The theme of Federico Fellini's film La Strada. The sad melody played on trumpet perfectly voices the pathos of the film.
Innovative music composed for Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho for string ensemble alone. The 'stabbing sound' (violin glissando) of the shower scene became a legend of film music.
Music for Hitchcock's Vertigo. Through endlessly circling arpeggios and unstable harmony, it perfectly depicts the protagonist's vertigo and obsession.
Herrmann's last work, written for Martin Scorsese's Taxi Driver. A jazzy saxophone solo expresses the city's night streets and the protagonist's loneliness and madness.
Released in 1966, the first Korean electronic music (musique concrète). An experimental work composed by recording and altering everyday sounds (water drops, machine noises and so on).
A chamber work for flute, piano and percussion. One of the early representative works of Korean avant-garde music, influenced by Isang Yun, Stockhausen and others.
A representative art song by Na Un-young. Set to a poem by Kim Tae-o, it portrays the lyricism of a moonlit night in a Korean pentatonic melody.
A representative hymn of Korean church music. Composed on the text of Psalm 23, it is widely sung as a four-part chorus.

A children's song set to a poem by Han In-hyeon. Beginning with the words 'Mother, in the island's shade...', its lyrical, plaintive melody has gone beyond the children's song to become a favourite of the whole nation.
A representative art song by Lee Heung-ryeol. It is marked by a solemn melody that expresses the han (deep-seated grief) of the people through the image of crossing a hard, rocky hill.
Beginning with the words 'Forgetting all the pain of giving birth', a song that symbolizes Parents' Day. A devout art song about a mother's sacrificial love.

Jo Doo-nam's most famous gagok, beginning with the words 'The green pine of Ilsongjeong...'. It is said to portray the independence fighters of the Manchurian plain, but there is controversy over the background of its words and music (pro-Japanese collaboration).
A lyrical gagok beginning with the words 'Whenever I see you...'. It is marked by a tender melody that longs for one's hometown and first love.
A version of the 'Air', the second movement of Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 3, arranged to be played only on the violin's lowest G string. Its calm, sublime melody is characteristic.
The most famous chorus among Bach's church cantatas. A flowing triplet accompaniment and a serene choral melody blend together, and it is often used at weddings.
A piece that often appears in solemn scenes of films and dramas. The stately, solemn rhythm of the Baroque dance and its intense chord progression are striking.
The largest and most famous of Mozart's horn concertos. The lively rondo theme of the third movement, reminiscent of a hunting horn, is widely known.
A sonata Mozart wrote for beginners, which carries the subtitle 'Sonata facile' (easy sonata). The clear, pure opening of the first movement is a melody everyone has heard at least once.
Known as the 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star Variations'. Based on a French folk-song theme, it is a lovely piece that unfolds twelve varied, virtuosic variations.
Programme music in which Beethoven depicts the feelings he experienced in nature. The sounds of a brook, birdsong, a storm and more are vividly expressed by the orchestra.
A piece whose rhythmic drive is so striking that Wagner praised it as 'the apotheosis of the dance'. The second movement, with its solemn, mysterious atmosphere, is especially popular.
The brightest and warmest of Beethoven's violin sonatas. Its beautiful melodies carry the lively spirit of spring.
A masterpiece among Beethoven's middle-period sonatas, in which passionate, stormy emotion sweeps through. It demands a high level of technique and a powerful touch.
A work Beethoven dedicated to his patron, Archduke Rudolph. It is considered the most grand and noble masterpiece in the history of the piano trio.
The most famous of Boccherini's works. It is a model of the elegant, aristocratic Rococo style, and the delicate shimmer of the strings is beautiful.
A song Schubert composed on an epic poem by Walter Scott. Thanks to its devout, beautiful melody, it is often performed in religious contexts as well.
The best loved of Schubert's short piano pieces. Its charm lies in a simple, folk-like melody set over a light accompaniment.
Published after Chopin's death, it is famous as the theme of the film The Pianist. Its plaintive, sad melody touches the heart.
The longest of Chopin's preludes. The A♭ that repeats throughout the piece is reminiscent of raindrops falling from the eaves.
A piece about which Chopin himself said he had 'never written a more beautiful melody'. It is marked by a lyrical melody and a contrasting, passionate middle section.
Regarded as the greatest of Schumann's chamber works. The piano and string quartet are in perfect harmony, and it overflows with Romantic passion and energy.
A piece that stands out for Mendelssohn's characteristic flowing melodies and balanced form. The lyrical theme of the first movement, played by the cello, is especially famous.
A concerto that concentrates Liszt's brilliant virtuosity. Its active use of the triangle in the orchestra has earned it the nickname 'Triangle Concerto'.
The most famous lullaby melody in the world. Brahms composed it for a friend's child, and it carries a simple, warm feeling.
Brahms's last symphony, a masterpiece that combines classical formal beauty with Romantic tragedy. The fourth movement, which adopts the Baroque form of the passacaglia, is the highlight.
The most popular of Tchaikovsky's symphonies with the public. It portrays a struggle against fate and the victory over it, and the horn solo in the second movement is very beautiful.
Tchaikovsky wrote it out of admiration for Mozart. A masterpiece that stands out for its elegant waltz movement and the rich sonority of the strings.
One of Rachmaninoff's most widely known piano pieces. The contrast between the intense, march-like rhythm and the lyrical middle section is superb.
An early piano piece by Debussy, dreamlike and gentle in mood, as its title ('Reverie') suggests.
A violin piece Ravel made by borrowing the style of Hungarian Gypsy music (tzigane). A brilliant and difficult work that demands the highest virtuosity of the violinist.
A bright, lively piece that Shostakovich composed as a birthday present for his son. It became even better known through its use in Disney's film Fantasia 2000.
An early signature work of Elgar, full of English refinement and lyricism. The soft, warm harmony of the strings is soothing.
A piece that reinterprets Arirang, Korea's representative folk song, in a modern art-song form. It is marked by Korean sentiment and grandeur combined with piano accompaniment.

The first of the orchestral suites that Khachaturian compiled in 1943 from the music of the ballet Gayaneh, which is set on an Armenian collective farm. Between dances that draw on Armenian folk melodies and rhythms sits the lyrical 'Adagio of Gayane', which was used in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

Mahler's last completed symphony. In the first movement, which begins with a hesitant rhythm, life and death collide, and in the final Adagio the string melody gradually fades away into silence. Mahler died in 1911 without seeing it premiered, and Bruno Walter gave the premiere in Vienna the following year.

Mahler's longest symphony, in six movements and lasting more than an hour and a half. Under a plan to portray the stages of nature one after another, it begins with an enormous first movement; in the fourth movement an alto sings the 'Midnight Song' from Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, and it ends with a majestic string Adagio.

Incidental music written by Grieg for a production of Ibsen's play Peer Gynt. It premiered in 1876 in Christiania (now Oslo). 'Morning Mood', 'The Death of Åse', 'In the Hall of the Mountain King' and 'Solveig's Song' were later assembled into two orchestral suites and became more widely known.

Also called 'Actus tragicus', an early funeral cantata by Bach. It seems to have been written around 1707, in his early twenties, during his time in Mühlhausen. It begins with a quiet sonatina in which two recorders and two violas da gamba blend, and sings of a faith that accepts death.

A church cantata by Bach for bass solo. He wrote it in Leipzig in 1727 for the Feast of the Purification of the Virgin Mary, and it sings of the feeling that, like the old man Simeon holding the infant Jesus in his arms, one can now depart the world in peace. The swaying aria 'Schlummert ein, ihr matten Augen' ('Sleep now, you weary eyes'), No. 3, which is like someone lulling themselves to sleep, is especially famous.

A three-act opera seria that Handel wrote for the Royal Academy of Music in London. It portrays the fidelity of Rodelinda, queen of the Lombards, who grieves for her husband Bertarido, believing him dead, yet in the end refuses the marriage proposal of Grimoaldo, who has seized the throne. It premiered at the King's Theatre in London in 1725.

A symphonic poem inspired by Nietzsche's philosophical book of the same title. The 'Sunrise' introduction, in which a trumpet sounds C-G-C over organ and a low sustained note, is especially famous, and it became widely known through its use in Kubrick's film 2001: A Space Odyssey. Nine sections named after Nietzsche's chapter titles follow almost without a break.

A requiem for soprano and mezzo-soprano soloists, two mixed choruses and orchestra. It has four parts: Introit, Kyrie, Dies irae and Lacrimosa. The Kyrie (second movement), in which twenty voices interweave in micropolyphony, was used in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey. It premiered in Stockholm in 1965.

An unaccompanied mixed-chorus piece in sixteen parts. Setting the communion text of the Requiem Mass, 'Lux aeterna luceat eis' ('Let eternal light shine upon them'), the voices sing the same notes slightly out of step, so that the harmonies overlap and dissolve as if blurring. A representative work of Ligeti's micropolyphony, it was used in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

An orchestral work built not on clear melody and metre but on huge masses of sound. Each instrument takes a different note to form a dense cluster, and its colour and density change slowly. Premiered at the Donaueschingen Festival in 1961, it made Ligeti's name known and was used in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

The largest and most intense of Beethoven's violin sonatas. The violin and piano confront each other as equals, like a concerto. Beethoven first wrote it for the violinist George Bridgetower, but it acquired its present name when it was dedicated to the French violinist Rodolphe Kreutzer.

A piece for violin and orchestra that Saint-Saëns wrote for the Spanish violinist Sarasate. A melancholy introduction is followed by a rondo with Spanish rhythms that unfolds brilliant virtuosity. It is also often performed in the version for violin and piano arranged by Bizet.

Rachmaninoff's 1921 arrangement for solo piano of Kreisler's short violin piece Liebesleid ('Love's Sorrow'). To the wistful Viennese-waltz melody of the original he added his characteristic dark harmonies and countermelodies, making a piano piece that is deeper and more brilliant than the original.

Liszt's arrangement for solo piano of 'Widmung' ('Dedication'), the first song of Schumann's song collection Myrthen, which Schumann presented to Clara before their marriage. It keeps the song's melody intact while building it up with wide arpeggios and octaves, turning a declaration of love into grand piano music.

A piano duet for four hands that Schubert wrote in 1828, the year he died. It begins with a tender theme in F minor, passes without a break through a Largo, a Scherzo and a fugue-like finale, and returns to the opening theme. When it was published after his death, it was dedicated to his pupil Caroline Esterházy, whom he had held dear.

A collection of twelve piano pieces, one published each month throughout 1876, commissioned by the music magazine Nouvelliste. From January's 'At the Fireside' to December's 'Christmas', it portrays the scenery of the twelve months of the Russian year. June's 'Barcarolle' and November's 'Troika' are especially loved.

A sonata for piano four hands that Mozart completed in Vienna in 1787. It has a first movement in which the two players trade the themes with energy, a second movement that flows like song, and an elegant rondo as the third movement. It is a mature four-hand work in which the two parts confront each other as equals, like a concerto.

To a polonaise that Chopin had first written for piano and orchestra, he added a calm Andante spianato, written for solo piano in 1834, to make a single work. From the lake-still opening in G major it passes through a fanfare into the brilliant, majestic polonaise in E♭ major.

A suite in which Ravel orchestrated in 1911 his piano duet written for the young brother and sister of a friend. Based on Perrault's fairy tales and others, its five pieces, 'Pavane of Sleeping Beauty', 'Hop o' My Thumb', 'Laideronnette, Empress of the Pagodas', 'Conversations of Beauty and the Beast' and 'The Fairy Garden', depict scenes from fairy tales in delicate colours.

A chamber cantata by Vivaldi for alto solo, strings and basso continuo. Two recitatives and two arias convey the lament and anger of someone tormented by a heartless lover. The first aria, 'Ah ch'infelice sempre', in which pizzicato and bowed strings overlap in a sobbing flow, is especially famous.

Vivaldi's 'ripieno concerto', played by string ensemble and basso continuo alone, without a solo instrument. A short piece in three movements, fast-slow-fast, it condenses the characteristics of Vivaldi's concertos, such as vigorous rhythm and sharp contrasts of dynamics.

Vivaldi left more than thirty concertos for bassoon, and this is one of the more frequently performed among them. In the dark key of E minor, the bassoon shows both the weight of its low register and agile leaps, in three movements, fast-slow-fast.

A symphony Mozart wrote at 17. Only two of his symphonies are in a minor key, this one and No. 40, so it is known as the 'little G minor symphony'. The passionate first movement, driven by syncopation, became widely known when it was used in the opening scene of the film Amadeus.

A large-scale serenade in seven movements for twelve wind instruments and double bass. Oboes, clarinets, basset horns, horns and bassoons blend, and the Adagio (third movement) was used in the scene in the film Amadeus where Salieri, looking at the score, confesses that he seems to have heard the 'voice of God'.

Mozart's two-act opera to a libretto by Da Ponte. It portrays the debauchery and downfall of the philandering nobleman Don Giovanni, moving between comedy and tragedy. It premiered in Prague in 1787, and the highlight is the Act 2 finale, in which the Commendatore, now a statue, appears and drags the unrepentant Don Giovanni to hell.

Barber's arrangement for string orchestra of the second movement of his String Quartet, Op. 11, written in 1936; it was premiered by Toscanini and the NBC Symphony Orchestra in 1938. The slow melody builds step by step to a climax and then breaks off into silence, and the piece is often played at memorial occasions.

A song for which Mussorgsky wrote the music in 1865 to 'Sleep, peasant's son', a song from the play The Voyevoda by the playwright Ostrovsky. A Russian-folk-style lullaby for a peasant baby, it is one of his early songs, and two versions survive.

A sonata Mozart wrote in Vienna in 1781 to play with his pupil Josepha Auernhammer. A bright piece in which the two pianos share the themes and trade them, shining as if in competition. It is one of the few works Mozart left for two pianos.

A late work by Chopin named for the songs of the Venetian gondoliers. The left hand keeps up an accompaniment rocking like waves in 12/8, while the right hand sings a melody doubled in thirds and sixths. Written in 1845-46, it is his only barcarolle.

The first of the Op. 10 etudes, which Chopin dedicated to Liszt. The right hand runs ceaselessly up and down widely spread arpeggios across the keyboard, while the left hand supports it with a weighty bass melody in octaves. Because the hand must stretch wide, it is counted among the most difficult etudes.

Chopin's piano sonata, widely known for its third movement, the 'Funeral March'. The march was written first, in 1837, and the other movements were added at Nohant in 1839 to complete the work. After the passionate first movement, the scherzo and the Funeral March, the short finale in which both hands rush in unison is startlingly unconventional.

Chopin's last piano sonata, completed at Nohant in 1844. It has a more classical balance than No. 2, and passes through a majestic first movement, a light scherzo and a Largo that sings like a nocturne before ending with a fiery rondo finale. It is among the largest of his solo piano works.

An orchestral work based on Goethe's poem The Sorcerer's Apprentice. It vividly portrays the story of an apprentice who, while his master is away, uses a spell to make a broom fetch water and, not knowing how to stop it, floods the house, with a comic theme led by the bassoon. It premiered in Paris in 1897 under Dukas's own baton.

A symphonic poem that forms the 'Roman trilogy' with Fountains of Rome and Roman Festivals. Without a break it depicts four scenes of pines: at the Villa Borghese, near a catacomb, on the Janiculum Hill and along the Appian Way. At the end of the third section a recording of a nightingale is played, and in the fourth the march of a Roman legion approaches in a huge crescendo.

A three-act opera based on the legend of the Dutch captain cursed to wander the seas for ever, who is redeemed by the love of Senta, a woman faithful to the end. It premiered in Dresden in 1843 under Wagner's own baton. The overture depicting the stormy sea and 'Senta's Ballad' are famous.

A five-act grand opera about the tribune Rienzi, who in 14th-century Rome rose against the nobles to become leader of the people and then fell. Based on Bulwer-Lytton's novel, with a libretto Wagner wrote himself, its 1842 Dresden premiere brought him his first great success. The overture, which begins with a trumpet signal, is often played separately.

A three-act opera in which the knight Tannhäuser, who had given himself to pleasure in the grotto of the goddess Venus, reveals this at the Wartburg song contest, sets off on a pilgrimage, and is redeemed by Elisabeth's sacrifice. It premiered in Dresden in 1845, and for the 1861 Paris production Wagner newly wrote sensual ballet music for the Venusberg scene in Act 1.

A symphony to which Bruckner devoted the last few years of his life but which, because he died before finishing the fourth movement, remains in three movements. It is said to be dedicated 'to the dear God'. A mysterious first movement, a scherzo that hammers down roughly and a majestic Adagio follow, and it premiered in Vienna in 1903.

The Norwegian composer Halvorsen's arrangement for violin and viola duo of the passacaglia, the last movement of Handel's harpsichord suite in G minor, HWV 432. To the short theme of the original he added brilliant variations, making a concert piece in which the two string instruments trade breathlessly. It is also often played on violin and cello.

A concerto Mozart produced in March 1785, a month after completing No. 20 in D minor. Between a stately, march-like first movement and a light finale lies the second movement, an Andante, in which the piano sings dreamily over muted strings. The second movement was used in the 1967 Swedish film Elvira Madigan, and the film's name stuck as the concerto's nickname.

A two-act 'sailors' drama' that Mascagni wrote after the success of Cavalleria rusticana. Based on a novel by Alphonse Karr, with a libretto by Targioni-Tozzetti, it premiered at La Scala in Milan in 1895. It is rarely staged today, but the barcarola that follows the tenor aria is often recorded separately.
